summary:
Visitors in Nord-Est stand under the national framework of Italy. Same-sex relations are legal for men and women, the age of consent is 14 regardless of gender or sexual orientation, and cross-dressing is not an offence. Legal gender recognition has been available since 1982 and has not required sterilisation or sex reassignment surgery since 21 May 2015. On 23 July 2024 the Constitutional Court, in judgment no. 143, recognised non-binary individuals as rights-holders under Articles 2, 3 and 32 but declined to add a third registry marker, holding that only Parliament can alter the male/female binary; the same judgment struck down judicial authorisation for gender-affirming surgery after a legal sex change. On 14 April 2025 the Supreme Court of Cassation ordered identity cards to use the gender-neutral term "genitori" rather than "mother" and "father" for children with same-sex parents.

Protection against discrimination remains sectoral. No Italian law explicitly bans transphobic discrimination, and ILGA-Europe's 2021 report noted the absence of nationwide coverage of goods and services, leaving transgender people exposed in housing, education and health care. Employment discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation has been illegal since July 2003 under Legislative Decree no. 216 of 2003, with the police, armed forces and rescue-service exemptions removed by Law no. 101 of 2008. A Rome court ruled on 15 January 2023 that dismissing a trans professor amounted to sex discrimination, and in March 2025 the Civil Court of Asti recognised, for the first time, physical and psychological harm resulting from homophobic mistreatment.

Official hostility is part of the environment. The Education Ministry omitted LGBTI persecution from its Holocaust Remembrance Day circulars for a second year, a cardinal publicly described homosexual acts as a mortal sin, and Human Rights Watch's World Report 2025 records political rhetoric hostile to LGBT people as contributing to a hostile climate. In the Veneto regional council, the governing majority embedded that orientation in regional education policy: motion n.340, passed at the 178th public session in Venice on 3 July, sits alongside deliberation n.92 of 14 October 2014, which committed the regional government to a mandatory "Natural Family Day" observance on the last school day before Christmas and rejected the aims of gender-awareness content. The official regional government bulletin carries the primary text of that deliberation.

ILGA-Europe's 2026 Annual Review documents that homophobic and transphobic violence continued during 2025, including organised dating-app entrapment schemes in which groups lure victims and then assault or rob them. Progetto Gionata characterises transphobia as the most severe and most widespread discrimination confronting transgender people in Italy, consistent with a pattern recorded by monitors rather than isolated incidents. The most serious traveller-specific finding remains the sexual assault of young transgender tourists in Campania; ANSA reports that convictions for the assault were upheld on appeal in April 2026, an outcome that affirms accountability for violence against trans visitors rather than impunity. State-agent violence has also been prosecuted: in July 2024 a Milan traffic officer was sentenced to 10 months for beating a transgender woman with a baton.

Detention is the sharpest region-relevant risk. In January 2010 Italy announced plans for one of the world's first dedicated transgender prisons at Pozzale, near Florence, converting a nearly empty medium-security women's prison for about 30 of the roughly 60 transgender prisoners then held nationally, mostly convicted of drug or prostitution offences; gay-rights groups welcomed the dedicated space and its psychological support. Repubblica reported in 2013 that the project was abandoned. Before it, and afterwards, transgender prisoners had been held in women's prisons, where they were often segregated for their own safety.

Repubblica's investigative report of 28 August 2013, "La doppia sofferenza delle trans in carcere", counted 69 transsexual prisoners across ten Italian facilities. Placement tracked legal sex, so female hormones could not be prescribed to prisoners who, according to their identity card, counted as men. Trans women were held in men's sections, and those who had already undergone sex-change surgery were destined for the women's sections. Where cells were lacking, trans prisoners were put in isolation, described in the report as the most inhumane way of preserving their safety. Protected sections such as the G8 section at Rebibbia in Rome and the protected section at Poggioreale in Naples imposed limitations, including on partner visits. The 2011 Terni case produced a different line: the Spoleto surveillance magistrate ordered the local health authority to pay for a prisoner's hormone therapy to guarantee psychophysical integrity; the ruling was appealed and a July 2012 appellate decision followed.

Italy recognises persecution based on sexual orientation or gender identity as grounds for asylum under the 1951 Geneva Convention and the EU Qualification Directive 2011/95/EU, and Decree-Law No. 130/2020, in force 22 October 2020, simplified asylum procedures and reinforced protection for vulnerable groups including those persecuted on those grounds.
tangentialFactors:
The Pozzale plan announced in January 2010 placed Italy among the first countries to attempt a dedicated transgender detention unit, and its shelving by 2013 means the practical arrangement that survives is the one the 2013 investigation described: placement by legal sex, with trans women in men's sections unless surgery had been completed. A visitor's detention exposure therefore depends on documents as much as on presentation.

Regional policy in Veneto runs against the direction of the national courts. While the Civil Court of Asti, the Rome labour court and the Constitutional Court have expanded recognition since 2023, the Veneto regional council's 2014 deliberation committed a regional government to a mandatory school observance framed against gender-awareness content, and the 2025 motion n.340 indicates the council majority continues to legislate in that register.

Entrapment schemes documented in 2025 are not limited to a single city or region, so a regional location does not lower the risk surface on dating and hookup applications.
localsOnly:
Deliberation n.92 of 14 October 2014 bound the Veneto regional government to a mandatory "Natural Family Day" observance on the last school day before Christmas, and the same deliberation rejected the aims of gender-awareness content; the primary text is held in the official regional government bulletin. Families with school-age children in the region encounter this directly.

For residents held in custody, the Terni ruling of 2011 offers a route to have hormone therapy funded by the local health authority on psychophysical-integrity grounds; the appeal and a July 2012 appellate decision mean the current weight of that precedent is not established by these sources.

Protected sections at Rebibbia in Rome and Poggioreale in Naples were available to trans prisoners in the 2013 reporting, with restrictions including limits on partner visits.
outOfScopeNotes:
Unresolved: the number of transgender prisoners in Italy after 2013 is not sourced. The figure of 69 across ten facilities dates from the 28 August 2013 Repubblica investigation, and the roughly 60 figure from the January 2010 BBC report; neither source carries a current count.

Unresolved: whether any dedicated transgender detention unit operates now is not sourced. The Pozzale project is recorded as announced in January 2010 and abandoned by 2013, with no later source in this inventory.

Unresolved: whether deliberation n.92 of 14 October 2014 is still implemented in Veneto schools, and whether motion n.340 of 3 July reaffirms or replaces it, is not established by these sources.
